The monitoring and enforcement systems currently operational on Pakistan’s motorways, particularly the M2 (Islamabad-Lahore Motorway), are a mix of traditional manual methods and limited semi-automated technologies. While these systems have contributed to some improvement in road discipline since the establishment of the National Highways & Motorway Police (NH&MP) in 2001, they remain largely reactive, labor-intensive, and insufficient to address the growing traffic volume and unique geographical challenges of the motorway.
The M2, spanning 375 km, is one of the busiest and most economically significant routes in the country. However, sections such as the

) continue to be notorious black spots due to steep gradients (6–8%), sharp curves, and high risk of brake failure. Historical data indicates that since the motorway’s inauguration in 1997, the Salt Range has witnessed over 350 accidents resulting in more than 200 fatalities, with approximately 90% of these incidents linked to brake failures in heavy vehicles. Recent studies analyzing 10+ years of NH&MP data on M2 have identified multiple black spots, including locations at 195 km, 223–229 km, 234 km, and 283 km, where careless driving, dozing at the wheel,
bursts, and mechanical faults (especially brake failure) account for over 80% of accidents. Drowsy driving alone contributes to around 33% of incidents in certain analyses.

Existing systems struggle with limited coverage, delayed response, high dependency on human resources, and inability to provide proactive, data-driven interventions. This chapter critically examines the major existing systems, their features, operational mechanisms, and inherent limitations, setting the stage for the proposed AI-powered Intelligent Vehicle Monitoring System (IVMS).

This is the most traditional and widely practiced method on the M2. NH&MP officers use handheld radar speed guns or laser-based devices to measure vehicle speeds during patrols. Violations lead to on-spot issuance of physical challans (tickets), verbal warnings, or immediate fines. Officers also conduct random vehicle checks for documents, mechanical fitness, and driver condition. Recent enforcement campaigns have focused on newly revised speed limits (e.g., cars/LTVs reduced to 100 km/h on motorways from previous higher limits as part of fuel conservation measures). Patrol vehicles (SUVs, cars, and motorbikes) are deployed at strategic points, and mobile teams respond to reported violations.
Officers can only monitor small sections of the 375 km route at any given time, leaving large stretches unmonitored.

Enforcement relies entirely on officer presence, judgment, and availability, which is affected by shift timings, fatigue, and resource constraints. Manual recording increases the risk of errors or corruption.
The process is time-consuming, often causing secondary traffic disruptions when vehicles are stopped on the shoulder.

No centralized real-time data for trend analysis or predictive policing. Studies show that careless driving (23–25%) and dozing (21–23%) remain leading causes, which manual monitoring fails to prevent proactively.

Implemented primarily in the high-risk Salt Range section for heavy transport vehicles (HTVs), buses, and passenger service vehicles (PSVs). Vehicles are grouped into escorted convoys led or supervised by NH&MP patrol vehicles. Strict

speed control (often reduced to 30–40 km/h in downhill sections) is enforced to minimize brake overheating and failure on steep 7%+ gradients. The system includes 24/7 ambulance and fire tender support, trained first responders, and coordination with Frontier Works Organization (FWO) for road maintenance. This approach aims to prioritize human lives by controlling vehicle flow through dangerous terrain with sharp turns and poor visibility in adverse weather.
Convoy formation and controlled movement increase journey time substantially, causing frustration among commuters and economic losses for freight operators.

travel, forcing lighter vehicles to overtake dangerously or use the wrong lane.
Not feasible for the entire motorway or high daily traffic volumes. It addresses symptoms (speed on slopes) rather than root causes like poor vehicle maintenance or driver fatigue.

With increasing traffic, the system creates artificial congestion and does not utilize technology for individualized monitoring. Recent incidents and public complaints highlight that while it reduces some accidents, it remains outdated and disruptive.

Accidents or breakdowns are reported primarily through phone calls to the NH&MP helpline (130) or the national emergency number 15 (Rescue 1122). Witnesses or involved parties provide location details (often approximate), after which the nearest patrol team is dispatched. Officers then conduct on-site investigation, first aid, traffic diversion, and FIR registration. Some integration with rescue service

Response times can range from 20 to 60+ minutes depending on patrol availability, traffic conditions, and accurate location reporting. In remote or low-visibility areas of the Salt Range, delays are even longer.

Under-reporting is common, as highlighted by WHO estimates (around 28,000 road fatalities nationally in 2021) versus lower official figures. This hampers accurate analytics and preventive planning.

NH&MP has deployed fixed and mobile automatic speed cameras, including Average Speed Enforcement (ASE) systems over road segments. These cameras capture images or videos of vehicles exceeding limits, record number plates (with growing use of Automatic Number Plate Recognition – ANPR), and support evidence for challans. Some integration with e-challan systems exists for issuing digital fines. The system has been expanded on major motorways, and AI-based monitoring pilots are being discussed for M1 and M2. Cameras also help in general surveillance and toll-related monitoring via M-Tag (RFID-based electronic toll collection).
While detection is automatic, verification, stopping of vehicles, and fine collection often still require manual intervention, leading to traffic congestion when officers intercept violators.
Cameras are not installed ubiquitously across all 375 km; gaps exist, especially in curved or remote Salt Range sections.
Drivers use techniques such as plate covers, following closely behind other vehicles, or temporary number plate changes.
Current systems lack real-time alerts to officers, automatic accident detection, or driver profiling. They do not address non-speed violations like drowsy driving or mechanical issues effectively.

Manual follow-up actions disrupt flow, and false readings due to weather or technical glitches can occur. Recent reports indicate that while speed cameras have helped reduce some accidents (up to 50% in enforced zones in certain claims), overall enforcement efficiency remains low due to these gaps.

represent a foundational but outdated framework for road safety and enforcement. While they have reduced some violations through increased patrols and camera deployment, they suffer from critical shortcomings: heavy reliance on human resources, delayed and reactive responses, limited geographical coverage, high potential for evasion, and inability to leverage modern data analytics or artificial intelligence.

Particularly in high-risk areas like the Salt Range, where steep gradients and driver fatigue cause the majority of fatal accidents, these systems fail to provide proactive, scalable, and efficient solutions. National statistics reveal persistent gaps between reported and actual road crash impacts, underscoring the urgent need for modernization.

addresses these deficiencies by shifting to an automated, smartphone-centric, and intelligent ecosystem. It promises real-time monitoring, instant alerts, automated enforcement, and predictive capabilities, ultimately enhancing safety, reducing congestion, and supporting NH&MP’s mission more effectively.
